items.body: REWORK have been around long enough to know that club music’s supposedly clean breaks with the past are usually rather messier affairs. Michael Kübler and Daniel Varga formed the Stuttgart electronic project in 2000 with French vocalist Laetitia Rometsch, releasing their first EP, Anyway I Know You, through Frankfurt’s Playhouse Records. Their 2003 debut album, Fall Right Now, brought together early cuts, including “You’re So Just Just,” and established the combination they would come to describe as “new wave house”: spare machines, clipped funk, European pop instincts, and vocals that regard seduction as a form of mild antagonism. Later records for Playhouse, Visionquest, Get Physical, and their own Exlove imprint continued to complicate the boundaries between house, techno, electro, and pop at a time when those distinctions still carried considerable tribal weight. Released through Exlove Records on July 17th, the three-track Disco Love Remixes EP returns to the title track of REWORK’s March 2025 release. The original followed 2024’s Never Again and a Get Physical release that paired REWORK’s updated version of “You’re So Just Just” with separate remixes by Cinthie and Seth Troxler with Ryan Crosson. The new collection brings together interpretations by Neu-Romancer and Jennifer Touch alongside REWORK’s own “Disco Love2,” a special edit that reaches back toward the economical architecture of their Playhouse years. Sira Kübler’s vocal gives “Disco Love” its human temperature, sitting against bass and percussion disciplined enough to make each small adjustment feel consequential. The Playhouse influence is explicit in “Disco Love2,” although the track avoids becoming an exercise in period reconstruction. Its disco vocabulary has been pared down until glamour becomes something harder, stranger and slightly severe. Neu-Romancer is the solo project of Laura Bailey, an Australian musician, producer and DJ originally from Fremantle and now based in Berlin. Her 2023 debut EP, Neue Romantika, appeared on Zanias’ Fleisch Records, drawing on Italo disco, darkwave, EBM, and New Romantic references across four original tracks and a Zanias remix. The record included “Remnants,” a collaboration with Kris Baha, while Bailey’s broader history includes playing bass with goth outfit VV & The Void and punk band CIERN, as well as performing in Zanias’ live group. Her connection with REWORK predates the present remix: the artists released the two-track Call You Up EP together in June 2025. For “Disco Love,” Neu-Romancer takes the material into a more insistent space. Her remix thickens the rhythmic motion and introduces a bouncing, almost predatory momentum, making the track feel as if it were designed for the point in a club night when conversation has ceased to be useful. Details accumulate without clutter, and the arrangement maintains a peculiar forward pressure even as its gestures become more expansive. Neu-Romancer Jennifer Touch is a Berlin-based producer, singer, live musician and DJ whose work draws in part on her upbringing in eastern Germany. After issuing her first solo record in 2014, she developed a body of work that moves freely between post-punk, industrial electronics, wave music and club production. Her albums Behind the Wall and Midnight Proposals appeared through FatCat Records in 2020 and 2023, respectively, followed by Aging at Airports through Fabrika Records in September 2025. She has also released music through Riotvan, Eskimo Recordings, and Live at Robert Johnson, and has collaborated with Curses and Paranoid London. Touch approaches “Disco Love” from another angle, bringing greater emotional abrasion to its polished frame. Her version pairs cold-wave textures with a forceful club structure, allowing tension to build around Sira Kübler’s vocals and the regimented percussion. The bass bears down with greater weight while the upper register remains brittle and exposed. It is an effective reminder of how closely post-punk’s severity and dance music’s physicality have always sat beside one another. Jennifer Touch That relationship between post-punk and dance music also explains the logic behind Exlove Records, REWORK’s own imprint. Its catalog moves between synthpop, house, techno, electro, post-punk and synthwave without treating genre boundaries as border control, with releases from REWORK alongside She Lies, Philipp Roller, Sugartin and A Youth. Across more than two decades, REWORK’s tracks have also been handed to Andrew Weatherall, Roman Flügel, Trentemøller, Magda, Paranoid London, Cinthie and Seth Troxler for reinterpretation. They have little need to prove their underground credentials. “Disco Love” sounds more interested in what can still be done with them. Listen to Disco Love Remixes below and order the EP here. items.body: Summer songs traditionally have an unfair advantage. They get cars with the windows down, imprudent decisions, swimming pools, romances improved by temporary geography. Soft Vein’s new single Another Summer seems suspicious of all that. Justin Chamberlain approaches the season as someone might regard an old photograph found in a drawer: with affection, perhaps, but also with the knowledge that whatever happened there has already escaped its participants. The title suggests recurrence, but Chamberlain sounds interested in what recurrence fails to restore. Another season comes around. The people inhabiting it have changed. The song, the final single from Soft Vein’s forthcoming All We’ve Known of Heaven, has some of the suave composure of Robert Palmer and the eccentric pop intelligence of John Foxx and Peter Gabriel. A rounded bass line moves beneath clipped vocal phrases and lush synthesizers, which periodically rise around Chamberlain without swallowing him. The staccato chant and hook are especially good, giving an otherwise sumptuous ballad a curious nervousness, as though somebody has prepared the perfect sentence and then discovered that speaking it aloud changes its meaning. This year, Soft Vein has moved further toward synthpop, although Chamberlain retains a detached, cerebral chill. Another Summer may be the most persuasive argument yet for that development: a beautiful arrangement can make emotional confusion more acute. The bass has an almost tactile roundness; the keyboards occasionally widen into luminous sheets; his voice stays exposed in the middle, stylish without becoming mannered. Every element appears to know exactly how much room it should occupy. Chamberlain sings softly, often close enough to conversational volume that his restraint becomes part of the song’s psychology. Soft Vein has always been interested in the humiliations of wanting something from another person: reassurance, sex, permanence, an explanation. Another Summer finds him contemplating communication; his delivery has the attractive uncertainty of a person willing to disclose something before deciding whether disclosure was wise. That divided temperament has followed Soft Vein from 2023’s Pressed in Glass through Through Blinds, the 2024 record that brought Chamberlain’s songwriting into sharper focus. The 2025 EP From Another Room, featuring remixes by Twin Tribes and Qual alongside covers of formative artists, offered a useful bridge. All We’ve Known of Heaven is now available for preorder ahead of its release through Artoffact Records. Soft Vein will mark the album with a September 11 Los Angeles release show at Zebulon, presented by Minty Boi, with Catherine Moan as direct support and Secret Attraction opening. Buy tickets here. Listen to Another Summer below and order the single here. You can pre-order Soft Vein’s forthcoming new album, All We’ve Known of Heaven, here. items.body: Across the vast American sprawl, post-punk and darkwave have taken root in cities throughout the country, with each local scene giving the music its own character. Among the rising bands within that wider movement, Casket Cassette and Stare Away represent two distant geographic poles: Los Angeles and New York City, the City of Angels and Gotham, relentless sunshine and after-dark intensity. This summer, the bands have closed nearly 3,000 miles of continental distance on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour, the Los Angeles project’s first headlining run. Constant Laval Williams and Ben Nelson first became friends when Stare Away joined a Casket Cassette bill at Sip Studios in Jersey City, where they discovered common ground in Joy Division’s rhythmic force and Ian Curtis’s songwriting, as well as recovery, poetry, and the desire to exorcise personal damage through catharsis of a crowd. Both artists entered the tour with their most substantial releases to date. Casket Cassette’s third album, Reducer, released June 12, turns experiences of erasure, constriction, recovery, and the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires into a ten-song study of what survives when a life and community have been pared back. Post-Punk.com followed the record’s development through Kiss Me Awake and Show Me a Sign, songs that brought Williams’s doomed romanticism into sharper electronic relief. On July 31, Stare Away released its seven-song debut, In Absence, via à La Carte Records, drawing on Nelson’s seclusion after sobriety, the depths of addiction, and relationships that continued to exert their pull. Its closing track, Familiar, gave those concerns one of the album’s most immediate expressions. Onstage, their geographical and musical differences sharpen the pairing. Casket Cassette channels the strange darkness that flourishes beneath Los Angeles sunshine through electronic pressure and doomed pop melody, while Stare Away draws on Gotham’s nocturnal velocity with tensile bass, urgent guitar, and the close physical charge of an early post-punk club. As the tour enters its final stretch, Post-Punk.com spoke with Williams and Nelson about the records that guided Reducer and In Absence, the friendship behind the tour, the cultures of their respective cities, and the collaboration already waiting beyond the final date: Ben, in absence, feels like a reference to the terms “In Memoriam” or “To Absent Friends”. What kind of absence does the title refer to, and what emotional or thematic thread holds the album together? The record is a massive reflection on the past couple years of my life. I definitely secluded myself from a lot of aspects of living in New York City so I could just focus and make progress on better finding myself after getting sober. I just disappeared for a while from going out and was working full-time at a job I absolutely hated. I looked at myself & how insane the state of the world currently is, and put everything into my craft to reflect my own mysteries, questions & realizations of isolation, depths of addiction, and relationships I’ve had that were very important to me. I think when you put your heart into something physical and artistic, people will truly relate rather than follow like a cheap social media posting scheme and will feel much more fruitful and fulfilling in the end. I feel like I discovered more about myself throughout the process of writing this record than I ever would if I hadn’t. The title track sums up the entire record and each following track dissects it in its own way musically and lyrically. Sitting with Mike Morello in the studio and putting so much time and emotion into each song really tied it all up with a bow. Ben, which artists, records, or musical periods were foremost in your mind while making In Absence? Or writers and filmmakers perhaps? To really narrow it down, New Order’s “Movement” demos and writing sessions, The Cure’s “Faith” home demos, and The Sound’s “Jeopardy” record are in my everyday rotation. When it came down to pure influence, I really wanted to write from a direction as a band involved in the first wave with a maturing mid-80s attitude. The sculpting behind what defined an emerging underground genre is what I’ll always strive for when writing. Experimental films and beatnik writers of the late 50s and 60s called me to think more of vulnerability in expression when it came down to writing the lyrics. Ben, was there one song that unlocked the direction of In Absence and helped you understand what the rest of the record needed to become? “I Can’t Escape Myself” by the Sound. Truly a masterpiece of a track in my opinion. The daily hysteria of living life on life’s terms regardless of situation or control over one’s ability to have an answer for everything that shapes our identities and emotions is kind of a beauty in a sense, which makes us all unique in our own ways. The album art shot by Julie Lodhy really captured that reflection literally. Constant, what first set Reducer in motion, and how did the album develop from that initial idea into the finished record? I’d been spending most of my time focusing on crafting standout singles (Bouquet, Broken Tomorrow, etc.), and I wanted to return to another cohesive project. Specifically, for album #3, I wanted to respond to the erasure, reduction, and alienation I’d been feeling after returning home to LA from graduate school at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, and in the wake of the LA fires. In a short period of time, my community of friends and my childhood home had both burned, shrunk, or vanished. It was a period of interpersonal, mental, and physical loss. I first explored these themes in the context of inward reflection, and then expanded into an examination of my past and my relationship to others. I also chose to incorporate increasingly poetic elements (such as references to Robert Lowell’s Skunk Hour in Kiss Me Awake, a poem in the interlude, and various lyrics that leaned more deeply into nuanced metaphor). The instruments ended up expressing rage, loss, and existential claustrophobia via the use of heavy basslines and aggressive drums, coupled with ethereal anthemic synths and the occasional heartfelt guitar line. What made me fall in love with the darkwave and post-punk genres to begin with was their ability to honestly express pain and darkness while also transfiguring that same pain into something beautiful and danceable. I can only hope this new album achieved that same duality. Constant, the word “reducer” suggests compression, subtraction, or stripping something to its essential form. What does the title mean to you, and how does it relate to the album’s songs? I think that you summed it up nicely. Like the choke-chain collar in the cover art, the title reflects a feeling of constriction (a minimization of self, community and environment). If you have the kind of brain that I have, life can sometimes feel like a series of “reductions” almost like pruning a bonsai tree to try to stay “right sized.” This has always been the case for me (especially as someone in recovery), but to have those reductions unwillingly extend into the world around me was intense. I think the songs all mirror this differently. I tried to let them be eclectic; sometimes disparate elements in conversation with one another are more comprehensive than similar elements. On songs like Kiss Me Awake and Melting Angels, there’s a wide-open purgatorial feeling that’s at odds with poignant, pared-down lyrics. A song like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) is a bittersweet memory, a bleeding echo of a whole. Show Me a Sign and Becoming burst past constriction into raw expressions of existential energy (etc.). Harmoniously, the album was mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios, who works almost exclusively with analog equipment. The process of mixing with analog machines is also a reduction of the nebulous revisions and additions of modern DAWs; when effects were baked into the stems, they were made singular and permanent. The same is true for Matia’s raw, minimalistic approach to tracking vocals on songs I recorded in-studio such as Becoming. The stems of some songs like Elegy were compressed together onto tape, and then re-digitized. Constant, which artists and records exerted the strongest influence on Reducer, and where can you hear those influences entering the album? There is always a plethora of artists within (and outside of) the genre influencing me. These, of course, include the giants whose footsteps we walk in (ie. Joy Division, The Cure, Bauhaus, Siouxsie, etc.) as well as the peers I have walking beside me (check out my Spotify playlist for reference). If I had to narrow it down for this specific album, I’d say: Charlotte Sometimes by The Cure, But Not Tonight by Depeche Mode (specifically the intro), the body of work by Sad Madona (who I’ve done two collaborations with (including on Reducer), and who I’ve been hanging out with when I visit the EU), the music of my buddy Jamison (aka Gossip Cult), indie and indie-adjacent bands I used to listen to when I was a kid (like Beach Fossils, Surf Curse, The Drums, etc,), The Smiths, Atmosphere by Joy Division, Crystal Castles, experimental acid/trance/house music I used to dance to at illegal warehouse raves downtown, Nitzer Ebb, Pagliacci by Leoncavallo, and various movie soundtracks. As a result, songs like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) blend post-punk and indie/alternative, while songs like Show Me a Sign or Apathy are darkwave with elements of electronica and EBM. All of these influences have allowed me to move in a new direction while staying true to my voice. Constant, you are also a poet, photographer, and filmmaker. How did those other disciplines shape the lyrics, imagery, or structure of Reducer? For me, all these disciplines come from the same source but are expressed in different ways, each appropriate for different moments/needs. They all allow us as human beings to try to source meaning from existence and our universe; a meaning we will never fully reach, but a beautiful process regardless. Photography and film rely on choice of subject and composition to craft visual narrative or provoke thought, while music relies on a similar, auditory gut-instinct. These instincts are also involved in poetry, but the act of writing and editing a poem requires a more microscopic cartography; everything must belong, every word must connect, every image must work against or for the conceit of the poem. Poetry is my first love. I’m obsessed with it. There’s a beautiful anarchy to it, yet an intentionality that I don’t find to be fully true in music or photography. Sometimes my lyrics are hyper poetic, and sometimes I want a break from the intense scrutiny required of poetry. Sometimes I just want to write an immediately understandable or quasi-cliché lyric for the catharsis of that immediacy; just want to say “I love you” or “I miss you” and not “your shadow lingers in the wake of my delinquent dreams.” Coming out of the Writers’ Workshop and being in the process of finishing my debut collection of poetry, poetry played a much larger role in this album than in the past. As I previously mentioned, there is a full poem in the Interlude; songs like Elegy and Kiss Me Awake both use rhyme schemes (or non-rhyming free-verse) in their lyrics and poetic imagery that is a new frontier for the fusion of poetry and music for me. I have a very vivid imagination; it can be very cinematic at times. I daydream a lot. When I was writing Reducer, photography and cinematography also informed the songs for sure—if I can’t imagine a visual narrative in my head while listening back to a song, then it’s probably not a good song. Structurally, I always want my albums to have a narrative arc as well. In the case of Reducer, I wanted to start with a feeling of stasis and constriction that then erupted into defiant forward movement. Constant and Ben, how did the two of you first meet, and what were your initial impressions of one another, both personally and as musicians? Ben: We met at the Jersey City date of his first US tour with Blood Club and dustbowlchampion at Sip Studios, it was so cool to be able to meet from being on complete opposite sides of the country, everyone was so inviting and kind and it was awesome being able to appreciate each others music. It was like going to a new school and kicking it off with another kid in class with similar interests. Constant: Ben and I met a few years ago on my first-ever national tour with Blood Club and Dustbowlchampion. I had already been aware of Ben’s music after finding it online and would religiously listen to “My Cathedral” and “Something Strange” in my car on the way to work, so I was psyched when Ben was booked to play with all of us in Jersey City. I think we hit it off immediately; I could tell Ben just got it, it being the reason we all do what we do as artists. It’s really cool when you meet someone and are on the same wavelength. Stare Away. Photo by Constant Williams Constant and Ben, did you initially connect through any shared bands, records, or influences, and what helped that first connection develop? Ben: Definitely comparing our distinguished sounds to similar bands we both enjoy, I think Joy Division would be a top example because we both love Ian Curtis’ writing from a poetic standpoint, we did hit the exhibit in New York City together which was an awesome experience. I always learn of new books and readings to pick up from him. I also think it’s because I am a bassist and he came from a background of being a drummer, so I think a lot of bands that have that heavy foundation of rhythm sections drove a lot of our similar musical interests. Constant: For sure, I think most people who make music similar to us can connect over a shared love of many of the same bands (like the ones I mentioned before). I think it also helped that we both come to music at a poetic and existential angle, and we both could relate in terms of recovery from substances and the perspective shift that is required. Constant and Ben, what first made you want to collaborate musically, and when did the idea of touring together enter the conversation? We haven’t collaborated yet but we definitely have a song in the works. I think every time we’ve seen each other, we’ve thrown around the idea of touring together because we love each other’s music, and it especially made sense now that both of us are with BLCKJEANS. Ben, what appeals to you most about Reducer, and which song from the record do you find yourself returning to most often? I think Constants approach on the arrangements were genius. The drum breaks feel lyrical, the combination of synth selections and vocal melodies reached a part of this genre that hasn’t been touched upon yet, and classic Casket Cassette elements cultivated into his best work. My favorite part of all this is watching and listening as an artist grows musically. It’s hard to put my finger on a single song because each song has its own unique skeleton, but I have to go with “Apathy” as the track that’s always running through my head on this record. Constant, what do you enjoy most about In Absence, and which song on the album has become your personal favorite? Beyond how catchy and danceable its songs are, I love how authentic and genuine the album is. I also really enjoy the combination of quintessential 80’s New Wave sounds with dark Post-Punk melodies. The title track and Faithless Hum are my top favorites. Constant and Ben, your music shares certain post-punk and darkwave foundations while retaining two distinct identities. What do you think makes the bands complement each other so well on the same bill? Ben: I think our high-energy performances are what make this tour so special; the riffs throughout the night keep the atmosphere intense with movement and bring a great amount of nostalgia you feel at a goth club or punk show that you can’t capture at other shows. Our deep connection with the fans is what’s most important to me, hearing how the music can move through the audience and watching kids get lost in their dancing with their eyes closed while we’re playing on stage is so cool being able to resonate that from the stage. Constant: I think we complement each other because we both bring a similar energetic performance style, matching high energy with a candid sincerity. Ben’s music leans more towards post-punk with moments of darkwave, while my music leans more towards darkwave with moments of post-punk. I think that also creates a “yin and yang” effect for our live shows; two sides of the same coin. Casket Cassette. Photo by Aaron Jay Young Constant, you come from Los Angeles, while Ben is based in New York City. How have the music scenes and cultures of those cities shaped your respective projects, and what similarities do you recognize between them? And what do you think is different? Ben: I think New York City’s music scene is so diverse, which makes it such a beautiful and thriving location for musicians and showgoers. You can hit a punk show, an electronic show, hardcore show, or jazz club in the same borough in the same night. It’s wicked, I love it. I think LA is quite the same besides the traffic haha, but I think the diversity of people and genres is the best and most important similarity of both cities, keeping live music thriving. New York City in general has a million places to find and take inspiration from. Taking late night subway rides can create a huge narrative story in its own way, walking in the parks and seeing all different types of fashion and taking everyone’s unique sense of expression and sensing love and unfortunate disparities throughout the air can present all kinds of thoughts and ideas to put down on paper, it becomes its own dimension and reality that spews inspiration for lyrics and especially beat and rhythm. The nightlife through dive bars and street festivities is an overwhelming resource of artistic relation. You can simply sit in a moment, look around, and take in so much that you can’t find anywhere else. I try to take the mood and energy of wherever I was that night or night before to the writing process to resemble the city’s grit and hardstyle energy that keeps it alive. Constant: I think growing up in Los Angeles has informed my music a lot. There’s a strange duality to the shiny movie stars, warm beaches, and perpetual sunshine that is surrounded by industrial decay, violence, and broken dreams. I think my music has a similar duality, being both deeply sad and deeply danceable. That’s a strange combo that (I hope) works. It definitely reflects how I grew up and who I am; I never truly fit into any one box. On the contrary, despite being visually more gothic and less “shiny” than LA, I feel as though the scene might be a bit less substantial in size in New York City, but I only know a little from my limited experience. It has always made me laugh that the places with the most goths are often the ones that punish us with bright sunlight (ie. Los Angeles, Mexico City, San Antonio, etc., with the exception of Chicago). I love New York, and I do think there is a kinship between the two cities, and certainly they are two of the most important musical hubs in the world. Constant and Ben, what are you each most excited about on this run, and what kind of experience do you hope audiences take away from seeing both projects in the same room? Ben: I’m really stoked to finally play these new songs live and also give the fans a chance to sing the songs that got us here with us. My absolute favorite part is inspiring younger showgoers to keep pushing their craft; the young musicians are the main reason I do this 100%. I started going to shows around 12-13 years old at VFWs and want to relive how I felt when people rushed to the stage to snag the mic from the vocalist to scream the lyrics. We want to go against the grain as much as possible so we get sweaty with everyone on stage with us during ‘Parting Ways’. It just started out of a last-minute call-up on our first show in San Diego so I just wanted to try and accomplish that every single night regardless of the size of the audience. I was pretty nervous at first, but I know the fans have such a fun time being able to dance underneath the lights with us, and that’s what matters the most. I hope the audience can take away a fresh new ear for Post-Punk music and can feel like they’re at a Factory or CBGB show. I just want people to feel free in a safe space and take home an amazing show experience. Constant: I’m excited to play shows with Stare Away and all our awesome local openers because I know the audience is going to have a great experience! As my first headliner tour, I’m also really excited to get to play a longer set for fans; I’m always bummed when someone comes up to say hi and is sad that I didn’t play a specific song; hopefully having a fuller set mitigates some of that disappointment. Another favorite part of tour for me is meeting the amazing people who listen to my music; none of this would be possible without them, and they mean everything to me. All I want is for them to have a night where they can let go and enjoy themselves during these crazy times. Constant and Ben, once the tour is over and both albums have had time to settle into the world, what does each of you have planned for 2027, and do you envision further collaborations? Ben: As soon as we get back, I plan on just getting right back to constructing the direction of the next record. I want to find the perfect hybrid kit to add to our live shows and just make something different. I feel like a lot of bands just get trapped in the same sound, playing the same riffs. I definitely want to get my head into a new book and maybe pick up some weird new hobby, but I think I just want to challenge myself towards a new direction to take Stare Away. Constant: I recently won a literary award, and as a result I will be releasing a book of poetry in 2027 called Elegy with Beautiful Child, available for preorder from Milkweed Editions. My lifelong dream (even before music) has always been to publish a book of poetry, so this is a really important moment in my life! There is also a Stare Away x Casket Cassette song in the works, and Ben and I are good friends, so it’s definitely not the last you’ll be hearing from both of us.§ Casket Cassette’s Reducer is out now. Listen below, and Order Here. REDUCER by Casket Cassette Stare Away’s In Absence is out now. Listen below and Order Here. In Absence by Stare Away The end of the Reducer tour leaves both artists with fresh work already taking shape. Nelson plans to begin developing the next Stare Away record as soon as he returns to New York, introducing a hybrid drum kit while pushing the project toward unfamiliar methods. Williams will turn toward the January 2027 publication of Elegy with Beautiful Child, his debut poetry collection and winner of the 2025–26 Jake Adam York Prize. A Stare Away and Casket Cassette song is also underway, extending a friendship that began on a shared bill into the studio. Before those plans take over, Casket Cassette and Stare Away have eight dates remaining together on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour. The itinerary continues August 12 at Beat Kitchen in Chicago, followed by Minneapolis, Denver, Salt Lake City, Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco before their shared run closes August 22 at Summer Fox Brewing – Tower in Fresno. Casket Cassette and Stare Away Reducer Tour Dates: August 12 — Chicago, IL — Beat Kitchen August 13 — Minneapolis, MN — 7th St Entry August 15 — Denver, CO — Skylark Lounge August 16 — Salt Lake City, UT — Kilby Court August 18 — Seattle, WA — The Black Lodge August 19 — Portland, OR — Holocene August 21 — San Francisco, CA — Kilowatt August 22 — Fresno, CA — Summer Fox Brewing – Tower Follow Casket Cassette: Instagram Spotify YouTube TikTok Bandcamp Follow Stare Away: Instagram Spotify YouTube TikTok Bandcamp The post Between Fallen Angels and Gotham Nights — An Interview With Casket Cassette and Stare Away on the “Reducer” Tour appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Welp. Better late than never. It's Kvlt Kolvmn's a-bit-more-than-halfway through 2026 best of list! Strap into your frostiest pair of dungaroos. It's gonna get wild.Black metal has had a very curious year for me. While I would say about half of the records I've listened to in the genre have felt like all-time bangers, the other half have put me to sleep. So in honor of that, I'll be presenting half a top 10 list. You're welcome. More awesome, however, is Boeli's incredible top 10, which features a handful of records I had yet to hear prior to reading his selections. Let's just say that good taste abounds as his list unfolds.But no more delay. Here are our iciest picks of 2026 so far.Stay frosty.-Jonathan AdamsTop Albums of 2026 So FarJonathan’s ListSaidan - Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s WristAs made plain when I waxed ineloquent a few weeks ago regarding the benefits of embracing the cringe in your life, I’m a BIG fan of Saidan. I would contend that their four album run thus far is one of the most consistently impressive in recent black metal, with each record refining and tactfully building upon what came before. Given this dynamic, it should come as no surprise that Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s Wrist is not only the band’s most complete and fantastic album thus far, but also the best extreme music record of the year so far. For me, it’s not close. What Saidan manages to channel here is a superb blend of melodic black metal, punk aesthetics, and power metal speed (replete with memorable hooks, punchy breakdowns, and manically aggressive tremolo shred sessions). It’s a relatively unique mixture that works due to genuinely gorgeous songwriting, which allows each sound to coexist seamlessly and interdependently without giving the listener genre-bending whiplash. The base is always black metal, and Saidan writes like a black metal band expanding the margins of the genre’s template with tasteful aggression. But their inclusion of other styles only works to sharpen and deepen listeners’ immersion in the world they’re creating. There isn’t a dull moment on this thing, and I frequently find myself hitting play again immediately after “Memory” fades into static. It’s addictive as hell. And, ultimately, that’s what I want from a record. I want to be transported, invited into a sonic world that’s cohesive enough to keep my undivided attention, and varied enough to never feel stale. And that’s exactly what Saidan provide with this absolute gem of a record. It’s my favorite thing I’ve heard so far this year, and I have a hard time imagining it being supplanted. Melodic black metal perfection.  FANGDRILLER: Scars Beneath Memory's Wrist by Saidan Miserere Luminis - SideraSpeaking of immersion, few albums so far this year have gripped me to the degree that Sidera, the third full-length from Montreal-based Miserere Luminis, has. Man oh man is this an exquisite slab of melody-heavy and deeply atmospheric black metal. The compositions are simply fantastic, winding and building into a delicious labyrinth of emotionally devastating delight. The musicianship on display here is also superb, allowing these tracks to breathe in the appropriate places before laying the black metal hammer down to glorious effect. It’s a fantastic showing from a band that has yet to release a dud, and I cannot wait to see where they transport us next.  Sidera by Miserere Luminis Worm - NecropalaceOne of the most hyped and ballyhooed records of the first half of 2026, I was honestly ready to judge this thing pretty harshly given initial impressions I’d heard from friends around the band's shift in tone. Happy to say I was dead wrong, as Necropalace feels like the most natural direction in the world for Worm to go after spending significant time with it. In a similar vein to Fangdriller, this record is just FUN. The songwriting is gothic and propulsive, creating an almost theatrical atmosphere that’s deeply enjoyable to sit in. One would never have guessed at Worm’s doomy roots by hearing Necropalace, thus is its genuine quality as a black metal album. Can’t recommend it highly enough, and plan on giving this thing many more spins throughout the year.  Necropalace (24-bit HD audio) by Worm Ultha - A Light So DimUltha is one of the most unpredictable and strangely amazing collectives working in the black metal sphere today, and A Light So Dim is unequivocally their boldest experiment to date. Thankfully, it works on almost every level. While the tonal shifts may look jarring on paper, Ultha’s unique skill of pulling various sound tapestries and weaving them into a robust whole is on full display here, and there isn’t a thing I’d change about this record. It is a long journey, which may be off-putting to some. But rest assured the time will be well spent. This is my favorite of the group’s records so far and a musical odyssey well worth taking. Genuinely brilliant stuff from these German geniuses.  A Light So Dim by ULTHA Misotheist - De PinteWell, enough pansy ass beautiful/experimental poser black metal, amirite?? JK naturally. While I’m a huge fan of bands that push the black metal formula to the fringes of trve, I’m still a devotee of the core sonic nastiness that made this genre the pariah it is in the music world. Enter Misotheist and their brilliant fourth full-length outing De Pinte. Like your black metal with a hefty dose of buzzsaw dissonance and tremolo violence? You’re in luck! This record absolutely slays. The first three tracks in particular are nothing short of a masterclass in black metal done right, with enough audio violence to sate even the thirstiest fan. But it’s the records fourth cut that shows the band’s capabilities most notably, presenting a doomier side that slows down the tempo but never once minimizes the menace or aggression these enigmatic Norwegians are known for. It’s a brilliant album that has received many a spin from yours truly and a true highlight of 2026.  De Pinte by Misotheist Boeli’s Kvlt kolvmn Top 10: Where Kvltvre Goes to Feed the Vvltvres10. Einherjer - LifebloodBy virtue of another folk-tinged black metal indebted band not making the cut for reasons of probable sketch, Einherjer just made my top 10 spot even though it’s hardly been out long enough to form a proper opinion.One thing I can say without hesitation, is that I quite enjoy the Norwegian Viking metallers trajectory since I last actively listened to them about a decade ago. While Av Oss, For Oss was an occasionally engaging if fairly monotone exercise in mid-paced black metal, Lifeblood is a much more colorful and generally more dynamic and melodic affair, and while still rooted in black metal, the branches of its world tree sapling have grown to embrace heavy metal and folk metal more and more. I appreciate their more melodic and varied approach, and would appreciate it even more with some more tempo variation and a bit of judicious editing. That being said, there are times I long for this subgenre like no other, and this year Einherjer have been its prime deliverer so far.  Lifeblood by Einherjer 9. Burnt Lodge / Veytik - Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split)Another somewhat late entry, I had almost completely missed this release, and was well and truly excited when I saw Burnt Lodge had new stuff out. Their 2024 release Intergenerational Anamnesis is one of my favourite iterations of Native American Black Metal. This particular micro-genre is a particular favorite of mine, and alongside Blackbraid and Nechochwen, Burnt Lodge sits among its top practitioners. Had this been a full album,. And had I discovered it earlier, this one might have sat quite a bit higher.While I also quite enjoy Veytik’s thrasher, Hellenic and Obsequiaesque escapades, they have not yet managed to grab me like Burnt Lodge does.  Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split) by Burnt Lodge 8. Pure Wrath - Bleak Days AheadI shall lazily refer you to my previous musings on Pure Wrath’s latest in Mays Kvlt Kolvmn.  Bleak Days Ahead by Pure Wrath 7. Stormkeep - The Nocturnes of IswylmOn their latest, bombasically titled album, Stormkeep took me by storm out of the gate, although I’m not yet wholly sure they’ll remain in my top 10 for the year entire. I generally like my black metal adorned with a serious amount of low-end, contrary to its traditional sound. While Stormkeep toe the line of what I enjoy production wise, the mix of spooky whimsy, expansive songwriting and exhilarating choruses managed to perk my ears up considerably. The gruff, charming and incredibly catchy gang shouts of opener “The Taste of Immortal Blood” are choice as hell, and while I could do with some more hooks like those to get my very mortal blood a-pumping in the mid section before the last two tracks offer a convincing coda, I suspect the album may need some more time to gestate before it truly settles in. The Nocturnes Of Iswylm by Stormkeep 6. Antrisch - Expedition III: RenitenzpfadAtmospheric black metal might be one of the most oversaturated and justly maligned sub-genres, but when done right, it can also be one of it’s most powerful. Of course your definition of “right” will vary, and there are many roads to Rome. Enter Antrisch, whose take on the sub-genre is one I would use as a prime example of doing atmoblack well. Antrisch unleash a vicious, razor-sharp blackened assault, while adorning their music with a powerful, iterative concept of (historical) exploration of some very inhospitable environments.While previous album Die Passage’s arctic voyage was an obvious fit for Antrisch’s icy timbre, Renitenzpfad might be equally if not more exciting for its less obvious theme of the hardships endured and horrors dished out by Spanish colonisers in the Americas. With all of Antrisch’s biting venom, this time empowered by topical and tasteful atmospheric interludes, sampling and thematic instrumentation, they once again succeed in telling a story and immersing their audience in it, without ever diluting their vicious, energetic core sound. Smart, urgent, dynamic and varied, while remaining remarkably cohesive;  Expedition III is another successful iteration in these Germans’ discography. EXPEDITION III : Renitenzpfad by Antrisch 5. Ashbringer - SubglacialI stand by my original review; anything close to 2019s Absolution would have topped any list, whether Black Metal specific or not. Time has both made me lost sight of Subglacial (who releases an album in January, I ask you!?), while also softening my initial dashed expectations for another long-form atmoblack magnum opus. My expectations should not make for a good or bad album in the end, and Ashbringer’s wintry yet somehow warm and nostalgic 2026 release is absolutely a good album. Go listen to it if you haven’t yet, and then go listen to Absolution.  Subglacial by Ashbringer 4. Apolaustic - No Plenitude Without SufferingWere it not for a scheduling snafu on my end, I would have reviewed this melodic black metal gem in April, and could now get away with another short referral to something I wrote before. Alas, no luck. I did not, and you shall now suffer my relative plenitude. I picked up the promo for this album based on a promising single at the time, and was further pleasantly surprised by an album that proved deep and expansive enough that I was still forming a full opinion by teh time the review deadline slipped through my powerless fingers. A couple months later, I can tell you with full confidence that this is my favourite “pure” melodic black metal album of the year so far, defining meloblack in the vein of something like Mare Cognitum or Houle. Decidedly less maritime (in title or sound) and with a much more space-faring vibe going on, Apolaustic’s ability to write dynamic songs with an undeniably kinetic mix of melody, technicality and songwriting chops should be no surprise to anyone who is familiar with project mastermind Romain Negro’s previous membership of excellent progressive/medloic/technical death metal band Stortregn.Indeed, comparing No Plenitude Without Suffering to Stortregn’s younger black metal sibling would not be entirely inappropriate, as it exhibits the same mix of soul, shred and sheer scope, if so far lacking absolute supernova’s like "Grand Nexion Abyss” or “Xeno Chaos”.For any enjoyers of melodic black metal of quality and pedigree unfuckwithable, look no further. But please do actually, there’s three more entries. No Plenitude Without Suffering by APOLAUSTIC 3. Hellripper - CoronachAs it stomps, gallops and jigs between fun, fury and a finisher of true grandeur, since I last covered it in April’s KK Helripper’s Coronach has proven both it’s endlessly engaging vibrancy, and its ability to engage so many of the things that can make a metal album great, but rarely show up on the same album. It’s fun, it’s solemn and majestic, it's catchy, it’s angry, it brims with energy and sounds like it’s about to rip out of its restraints, but never gets speed metal sloppy. Incredibly varied yet uniformly great, Coronach should show up in quite a few lists come year’s end, and not just the blackened ones.  Coronach (24-bit HD audio) by Hellripper 2. The Silver - Looking Glass Hymnal BlueI honestly have no idea if this is even black metal, which is also the only reason it’s not on number one. The Silver’s sophomore amalgamation of metal styles is the kind of breath-taking bricolage that makes me want to rip up my clothes and howl at the moon. Rooted in a deep romanticism, indulgent, baroque, gothic and maximalist yet never tasteless, this album embodies what I love in my heavy music while eschewing everything I don’t.Considering its members comprise veterans of Horrendous (recognize those eardrum-flayingly awesome shrieks yet?) and Crypt Sermon, the quality is perhaps not as surprising, but while neither of those other projects fully mesh with my preferences, this one really, really does.The only criticism I would level at it is that “Tow Candles” and “My Lone Dark Lantern” are simply so good that they threaten to cast shadows as dark as their lights are bright, and thus obscure their surrounding companions.  Looking Glass Hymnal Blue by The Silver 1. Miserere Luminis - SideraBut of course, my pride as a genre stickler could not survive placing anything at number oen that is not unequivocally BLACK METAL.Luckily, there is nothing disingenuous about this placement. Miserere Luminis, another stellar band out of Quebec (seriously, what’s the secret??) gracefully take the year’s twisted yet mesmerisingly beautiful throne. With an ear for blackened melodic rapture akin to Houle, riffs as snaky and entrancing as late-stage Ulcerate and the soul-rending cathartic qualities of Selbst,Sidera goes above and beyond its influences, featuring truly engrossing compositions replete with strings and probably my favorite drumming of the year so far. Gorgeous, sad and fragile without losing the razor-sharp bite that atmospheric black metal so often lacks, I have no doubt this tour-de-force will remain at or near the top come final list season, and stay in rotation far beyond the year’s end. Sidera by Miserere Luminis

items.body: 2026.08.12 生涯で取り組んだオペラは20作以上!? シューベルトといえば、「歌曲の王」として《魔王》や《冬の旅》などの代表作が挙げられるほか、数々のピアノ曲も愛されています。しかし、実は約20作ものオペラに取り組んでいたことはあまり知られていません。 しかも、シューベルトは14歳で最初のオペラを書き始め、亡くなる前年まで創作を続けるほど、このジャンルに情熱を注いでいました。それほど力を入れながら、なぜシューベルトは「オペラ作曲家」として成功できなかったのでしょうか。 シューベルトのピアノ作品全曲演奏をライフワークとするピアニスト・佐藤卓史さんのお話をもとに、その理由を探ります。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る ※本記事はポッドキャスト番組『ONTOMO Radio』で語られた内容を再構成しています。 佐藤卓史（さとう・たかし） 第11回シューベルト国際コンクールでの優勝と、その後の世界的な演奏活動を通して“現代随一のシューベルト弾き”の名声を確立。展開中のライフワークプロジェクト「佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス」では、未完成作品の補筆を含む前人未踏のシューベルトのピアノ曲全曲演奏に取り組み、注目を集めている。 秋田市生まれ。高校在学中に日本音楽コンクールで優勝。東京藝術大学を首席で卒業後渡欧、ハノーファー音楽演劇大学、ウィーン国立音楽大学で研鑽を積む。その間、ミュンヘンARD国際コンクール特別賞、シューベルト国際コンクール第1位、シドニー国際コンクール第4位・ショパン特別賞、エリザベート王妃国際コンクール入賞、カントゥ国際コンクール第1位、メンデルスゾーン国際コンクール最高位など受賞多数。ウィーン楽友協会をはじめとする欧州各地のコンサートホールに出演のほか、2011年にはシリア・ダマスカスのダール・アル・アサド文化芸術劇場でソロリサイタルを開催。 NHK交響楽団、東京交響楽団、日本フィルハーモニー交響楽団、山形交響楽団、仙台フィルハーモニー管弦楽団、神奈川フィルハーモニー管弦楽団、大阪交響楽団、広島交響楽団、ベルギー国立管弦楽団など内外のオーケストラと多数共演。「トリオ・ジャパン」（with石田泰尚・西谷牧人）、「トリオ・スペリオール」（with泉原隆志・上森祥平）各メンバーを務めるなど、アンサンブルピアニストとしての活躍は特に知られており、著名アーティストから絶え間ない共演オファーが寄せられ続けている。 近年は作編曲の分野でも活動を本格化させるほか、放送・配信・執筆・レクチャーなど幅広いフィールドで音楽の“楽しさ”と“奥深さ”を伝える活動に力を注いでいる。 www.takashi-sato.jp シューベルトが本当に目指していたのはオペラ作曲家 シューベルトが最初にオペラを書いたのは14歳のとき。その後も生涯を通して創作を続け、完成作だけでも8作品ほど、未完作なども含めると約20作品に及ぶといわれています。 佐藤さんによると、シューベルトは生涯で使った五線紙の約3分の1をオペラに費やしたともいわれるほど。紙そのものが高価だった時代に、友人が五線を引くのを手伝ったという逸話まで残っています。 それほどまでにオペラへ情熱を注いだ背景には、当時の時代事情がありました。19世紀初頭、オペラ作曲家は作曲家の中でも‟花形”の存在。成功すれば名声も経済的な成功も得られる、憧れの職業だったのです。シューベルトもまた、歌曲だけでなく、オペラで成功することを大きな夢としていました。 シューベルト：オペラ《鏡の騎士》 なぜオペラでは成功できなかったのか しかし、その夢は生前には叶いませんでした。最大の理由として挙げられるのが、当時のウィーンではイタリア・オペラが圧倒的な人気を誇っていたことです。 ロッシーニをはじめとするイタリア人作曲家の作品が劇場を席巻し、ドイツ語によるオペラは観客を集めるのが難しい状況でした。シューベルト自身もドイツ語によるオペラを書き続けましたが、時代の流れはあまりにも厳しかったのです。 さらに、佐藤さんは「ドイツ語オペラそのものがまだ発展途上だった」と指摘します。イタリア語は母音が多く、劇場でも歌詞が伝わりやすい言語です。一方、ドイツ語は子音が多く、オペラとして歌うための表現方法がまだ十分に確立されていませんでした。 のちにワーグナーらが切り開いていくドイツ語オペラの世界は、まだ始まったばかりだったのです。 31歳という早すぎる死も大きかった もう一つ見逃せないのが、シューベルトが31歳という若さで亡くなったことです。歌曲は仲間たちの前で演奏し、その反応を受けながら作品を磨いていくことができました。 しかしオペラは違います。上演には劇場や歌手、大人数の演奏家が必要で、作品を書いても実際に舞台にかかる機会はほとんどありませんでした。 佐藤さんは、「経験を積み、上演を重ねることでオペラ作曲家として成長する時間が足りなかったのではないか」と話します。 また、シューベルト自身の性格も影響していたのかもしれません。目立つことを好まず、初演で舞台に呼ばれても表に立つことを断ったという逸話も残っています。 華やかな劇場文化の中心で活躍するオペラ作曲家という存在は、もともとの気質とも少し距離があったのかもしれません。 シューベルトオペラ入門におすすめなのは《アルフォンソとエストレラ》と《フィエラブラス》 かつては「台本が弱い」「劇的な展開に欠ける」と評されることも多かったシューベルトのオペラ。しかし近年では、その穏やかな物語運びや美しい旋律、ロマン派へとつながる和声の豊かさが再評価され、ヨーロッパでは上演機会も少しずつ増えてきています。 「これまで欠点と考えられていた部分が、実はシューベルトらしさだったのではないか」という見方が広がってきたのです。 そこで佐藤さんがシューベルトオペラ入門としておすすめする作品は、《アルフォンソとエストレラ》と《フィエラブラス》の2作品。 《アルフォンソとエストレラ》は、全編が音楽でつながる意欲的な構成を持ち、のちのワーグナーにも通じるような先進性を感じさせます。 シューベルト：《アルフォンソとエストレラ》 一方、《フィエラブラス》は中世の伝説をもとにした壮大な作品で、合唱を効果的に用いたドラマ性が魅力です。 どちらも生前には劇場で成功を収めることはありませんでしたが、現在ではシューベルトの新たな魅力を知る作品として注目されています。 シューベルト：《フィエラブラス》 シューベルトが描いた劇場音楽をピアノで味わえる！ 佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス第24回 「4手のための序曲 ―オペラの夢―」 日時： 2026年9月13日（日）14：00開演 会場： 音楽の友ホール 出演： 佐藤卓史、尾崎未空（ピアノ） 曲目： シューベルト／イタリア風序曲 ニ長調 D592、歌劇《アルフォンソとエストレッラ》序曲 D773、英雄的大行進曲 D885、イタリア風序曲 ハ長調 D597、歌劇《フィエラブラス》序曲 D798、エロルドの歌劇《マリー》の主題による8つの変奏曲 D908 詳しくはこちら 「佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス」企画第24回。今回のサブタイトルは「オペラの夢」。上記2つの代表作《アルフォンソ》《フィエラブラス》の序曲は、シューベルト自身がピアノ連弾用に編曲している。これが今回のメインで、加えて19歳のときにロッシーニの《幸福な錯覚》の上演を聴き、そのイタリア風の明るい響きに影響されて書いたという2曲の「イタリア風序曲」（やはり作曲者自身による連弾版）、またケルントナートーア劇場のコレペティトーア時代にオペラの挿入曲を書いていた作曲家エロルドのオペラ《マリー》の主題による変奏曲など、シューベルトのオペラとの関わりに焦点を当てたプログラムを取り上げる。 連弾で共演する尾崎未空はミュンヘン在住のピアニストで、日本ではPTNA特級グランプリでおなじみのほか、国際的に活躍中。2人だけでの共演は今回が初めて。 ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 後編もお楽しみに！ シューベルトに関する記事はこちら シューベルトに関する書籍

items.body: 2026.08.12 海外クラシックNEWS～from イタリア 海外のクラシック界のニュースやコンサート、オペラ公演の様子を、現地在住の筆者がいちはやくお届け。今回は7月のイタリアの音楽シーンから、2つのニュースをお届けします。 取材・文 取材・文 野田和哉 Kazuya Noda 東京生まれ。明治大学文学部を卒業後、1983年からイタリア在住、ピアチェンツァのG・ニコリーニ音楽院声楽科を卒業。30年以上前に『音楽の友』への執筆を始め、現在にいた... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 現存するイタリアが世界に誇る音楽家といえば、指揮者のリッカルド・ムーティはまちがいなくその最有力候補といってよいだろう。このほど、彼の功績を記念する硬貨が発行された。 7月15日にイタリア財務省造幣局が正式に発表したところによると、「単に彼の伝説的キャリアを祝うだけでなく、真の文化的アイデンティティの担い手に対しての認定として」発行するという。 3ユーロ銀貨で、純度は92.5パーセント。デザインは、表に彼の指揮姿、裏に彼の手とその背景に渦のような模様を配し、彼によって紡ぎだされる音の世界を表している。いずれもムーティの実際の姿を撮影した写真から起こしたデザインで、その顔と特徴的なジェスチャーから見てすぐにムーティとわかる。 この銀貨は財務省が発行する「著名なイタリア人」シリーズの一環ということで、彼のほかにもこのような栄誉を与えられたイタリア人はいるのだろうが、筆者はこのような記念硬貨やメダルにはあまり関心がないので、詳しいことは知らない。 ただ、筆者の手元にはジュゼッペ・ヴェルディの肖像を用いた2ユーロ硬貨があり、珍しいので保存している。かつてはヴェルディの肖像画が載った1000リラ紙幣というのがあったが、これは現在コレクターの間では結構高い値がつけられているらしい。この銀貨もやがてコレクターの垂涎の的になるのだろうか。 おりしもユーロの新紙幣では、ベートーヴェンやマリア・カラスの肖像が使われるという話があり、やがてムーティも紙幣になるのだろうか。 フェニーチェ劇場の合唱指揮者が交代 9月からフェニーチェ劇場の合唱指揮者に就任するエレナ・ピエリーニ © Fenice di Venezia ヴェネツィアのフェニーチェ劇場の次期音楽監督として指名されていたベアトリーチェ・ヴェネツィが、就任する前に解任されるという異常事態になっており、いまもって誰が音楽監督になるのか不明のままだ。そういう状況のなか、もう一件の人事をめぐって問題が起こりそうだ。 今シーズンの終了をもって任期満了を迎える合唱指揮者アルフォンソ・カイアーニの後任として、9月からエレナ・ピエリーニが就任するという発表があった。ところがこの人選をめぐって、合唱団の二つの労働組合の一つが「われわれになんの相談もなかった」として反発しているという。彼らはカイアーニの契約延長を希望しており、それについて劇場側との意見交換等を求めているようだが、もう一方の組合は「合唱指揮者の人選に合唱団が関与することはもともと規定に定められていない」として、この交代に異を唱えない姿勢を見せている。この点においてヴェネツィの件とは状況が大きく異なるわけだが、報に接した者としては、「またか」という印象はぬぐえない。 今年9月から就任予定のピエリーニはフィレンツェ出身、2017年からオーストリアのリンツの劇場で合唱指揮者を務める。イタリアの劇場での活動は今回が初めてではなく、サルデーニャ島カリアリの劇場で合唱指揮を務めた。ヴェネツィアでの初仕事は、今年9月にマリブラン劇場でレオンカヴァッロ《道化師》の合唱を指揮する予定で、公演の指揮はダニエレ・カッレガーリ。 退任するカイアーニはどこに行くのかというと、南イタリアのバーリにあるペトゥルッツェッリ劇場の合唱指揮者に就任することになっている。 来シーズンのフェニーチェ劇場のプログラムについては、新制作だけをここで紹介したい。開幕11月13日にジョルダーノ《フェドーラ》、来年2月にフンパーディンク《ヘンゼルとグレーテル》、6月にアントニオ・スマレーリャ《イストリアの結婚式》、9月にヘンデル《パルテノペ》、続いてベッリーニ《ノルマ》が予定されている。そのほか、新規ではないが注目したいのは、シーズン最後の演目となるチレア《アドリアーナ・ルクヴルール》だろうか。

items.album: Filtro ~ Structura Parva
items.excerpt: Structura Parva — literally “small structure” — acts as both title and manifesto. Seven years after Forma, the Italian duo Filtro (Luca de Biasi and Angelo Bignamini) have moved away from long-form improvisations built from concrete sounds and electrical interference towards something more concentrated, deliberate, and architectural. items.body: Structura Parva — literally “small structure” — acts as both title and manifesto. Seven years after Forma, the Italian duo Filtro (Luca de Biasi and Angelo Bignamini) have moved away from long-form improvisations built from concrete sounds and electrical interference towards something more concentrated, deliberate, and architectural. Across six concise pieces, they construct miniature sonic ecosystems from the sparsest of materials, embracing self-imposed limitations as catalysts for invention. Working with only a handful of sounds per track, Filtro adopt an approach reminiscent of Oulipo’s creative constraints, treating composition as a process of exploring the possibilities contained within a tightly defined framework. Yet the result never feels academic. The sounds themselves remain stubbornly alive: intermittent clicks, fragile drones, processed acoustic fragments and high-frequency traces evolve, misbehave and interact in ways that resist predictable looping or repetition. Rather than expanding ideas through scale, Filtro trace how small gestures ripple through space, giving the EP a sense of depth and movement. What distinguishes Structura Parva is its refusal of sonic flattening. Every sound retains its material presence and tactile character, whether emerging from a sampler, field recordings or processed everyday objects. The duo’s attention to dynamics and spatial placement ensures that even the sparsest passages feel animated by hidden tensions. These are not static minimal compositions but living structures, constantly shifting beneath the surface. The EP’s subtitle of sorts — “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets” — feels apt. There is a subdued melancholy running throughout the record, but also curiosity and attentiveness. By reducing their palette and abandoning improvisation in favour of meticulous composition, Filtro have created their most focused work to date: a quietly compelling study in how much emotional weight can be carried by the smallest of structures. In the following interview Angelo Bignami and Luca de Biasi explain their working process. Structura Parva feels like a significant shift from the long-form improvisation for concrete sounds and electrical interferences of Forma towards much shorter and more concentrated pieces. What led you to embrace these “small structures”? Was this reduction a deliberate aesthetic decision or the natural outcome of your evolving practice? Luca de Biasi: After Forma, we took a long break to dedicate ourselves to our solo work, which also gave us the opportunity to reflect on what we wanted Filtro to become. The idea was to work meticulously on individual sounds, processing them and finding affinities with other sounds to shape the pieces. We set a strict limit: just two sounds each and nothing else. The biggest change for me was using a sampler, which allowed me to process sound differently than in the past and focus on individual sounds before looking at the whole picture. We also worked extensively on dynamics and the movement of sound in space. In some tracks, this remained direct, while in others we added the natural echoes of the different environments where we re-recorded the pieces. Angelo Bignamini: It was a bit of both. It represents an evolution of our sound, moving away from what were initially uncontrolled, improvisation-based impulses toward actual composition focused on a few core elements. I believe this shift was influenced by our shared listening habits at the time, as well as a mutual desire to produce something more focused and structured. The EP is described as reflecting a new approach to “minimal structures and small electronics.” What does “small electronics” mean for Filtro in practical and conceptual terms? Are you interested in intimacy, scale, fragility, or perhaps a different relationship between sound and space? L: The new approach was all about working on individual sounds before the whole composition. In practice, I used a modular synthesizer consisting simply of an oscillator, a complex envelope, and a filter, constantly tweaking the sound until I achieved a satisfactory result. I did the same using very simple field recordings. As I mentioned, the choice of individual sounds, their interaction, and their interconnectivity were the core ideas behind the project. A: It is called “small electronics” simply because the entire project is built on just a few elements—each track develops across two or three layers at most—and an extremely minimal setup. Often, we are just using everyday objects or small acoustic instruments, which we record and process using a sampler and a laptop. The core idea was to maximize the value of each individual sound and distribute it throughout the space, which inevitably transforms both its signifier and its signified. Both of you have long been interested in sound detached from its original context and meaning. On Structura Parva, the sounds often seem stripped down to traces, gestures and subtle interactions. How do you decide when a sound has been reduced enough, and how do you prevent minimalism from becoming merely an exercise in subtraction? L: For this latest project, each individual sound was developed separately by Angelo and me. We both worked on our own ideas without any prior agreement. After months of work, we decided it was time to meet up and listen to what we had done. Choosing which sounds to use was ultimately quite simple and quick. I don’t know how, but the work each of us had done seemed to share a common goal. A: Honestly, I didn’t really worry about that problem. The goal was simply to find minimal structures that could convey emotional meaning—which, in a way, is a prerequisite for any kind of music. There is almost always a rhythmic element, a background texture or drone, and a melodic element. If you look past the totally hallucinated style, we aren’t actually that far off from a traditional song structure. Angelo’s work frequently explores deterioration, tape processes and feedback, while Luca’s practice involves modular synthesis and improvisation. How has the dialogue between these approaches changed since Forma? Has the balance between improvisation and composition shifted over the years? L: Our approach has always been improvisational. We used to meet for long sessions and then extract the sections that would become the final work. This time, it was different: we worked on the tracks individually, then discussed them and decided together which parts made sense when combined. We then re-recorded them in various environments to give them depth. We also placed great importance on the movement of sounds in space. Therefore, this latest work is much more compositional than our previous ones. A: In this latest work, there is absolutely nothing improvised. We worked in perfect sync on the individual tracks, with each of us utilizing our own sounds and processing techniques. What united us was a shared vision to produce something simple and circular, yet containing an internal evolution driven primarily by how the individual layers intersect. Nothing was left to chance, except for the deliberate use of random modulations and stereophonic automation. The EP is presented as “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets.” There is a strong sense of restraint and suspended tension throughout the six tracks. Were there particular emotional states, environments or listening situations that informed the album, or do you prefer to leave such associations entirely in the hands of the listener? L: There were certainly external factors that influenced the choice and development of the sound—not necessarily musical ones. In my case, books had a significant impact, changing my approach to life and, consequently, to music. Using a sampler also definitely allowed me to focus more on single sounds. However, I prefer not to give listeners any specific direction regarding our influences, so that their listening experience remains entirely unique and personal. A: The way people interpret tracks is one of the most incredible wonders of music. Because of that, I prefer to let listeners filter the pieces however they choose and place them in whatever context feels right to them. Personally, I feel these sounds express themselves best in a nighttime setting, but that is by no means a strict rule. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One could say that everything was building up to the emergence of Starsailor, like the base of a massive pyramid tapering to a razor-sharp point, at once provocative and evocative, where Tim found the true meaning of his existence. Psychology speaks of the "primal scream" for good reason; sometimes, one must undergo a certain process, a cathartic one, perhaps, to reach one's destination. Tim Buckley's destiny lay in the stars, yet he had to get there by traveling a long road; folk and jazz guided him toward that atonal, distorted, avant-garde present where he built his sanctuary alongside his inseparable partner, Lee Underwood.In Come Here Woman, John Balkin played the bass furiously, while Lee Underwood experimented on guitar with dark, almost operatic flamenco-style melodies, and then Tim began to sing, as he never had before... and never would again. A singular shooting star that, if you didn't see or hear it... you missed it.Then the music kicks in, and you have to jump on board, it's rock 'n' roll, too; the percussion and guitar take on a jazzy, yet atonal, quality, as does the electric piano. It's all a storm that catches us by surprise, blink, and you'll miss it."I Woke Up," accompanied by the horns, feels like waves crashing against the beach sand and receding; the muted trumpet and double bass are the perfect companions. Tim's voice shifts, sometimes a tenor, other times higher-pitched, but it is always exactly right, creating a relaxed summer vibe even amidst this strange, dreamlike atmosphere. Throughout the album, we never quite know what time or place we inhabit, yet we know we are truly there."Monterey" is an acoustic rock track, with jazz undertones, where Tim's voice takes the place of the electric guitar and its solos. It features peaks and valleys, ranging from whispers to moments where his voice, striking a high note, sounds almost like a saxophone. He is like a Californian Peter Hammill; while Lee Underwood kept the guitar going with ceaseless repetition, it was Tim who handled the variations. Far from being chaotic improvisation, there was indeed chaos, yet it was a chaos driven by melody, moving perfectly toward its climax."Moulin Rouge" is a lovely interlude sung in French, showcasing the beautiful voice he was known for, accompanied by the trumpet. "Song to the Siren" and "Jungle Fire" represent two extremes of his vocal range, the former restrained yet outwardly expressive, the latter a long build-up culminating in an explosion alongside the band, where his voice truly functioned as just another instrument amidst wild, guttural, and primal improvisation. This trajectory leads to the title track, "Starsailor," which evokes a space-like atmosphere, one that feels as though it is tumbling into a black hole, featuring vocal stylings that range from Zappa-esque lows to Hammill-esque highs, yet serve a vastly different purpose; the mood steers the song toward a progressive sound, far removed from the jazz style found at the album's start.The Healing Festival revisits free jazz, pure double bass and saxophone, with Tim himself singing, stretching his voice and warping it like a rain-soaked blanket that changes shape once it's wet. "Down by the Borderline" ends with a flamenco flair, just as it began, but featuring the trumpet. Then the guitar kicks in with an unstoppable groove, joined by the drums and Tim, who is practically prancing with sheer delight just listening to them set the stage. He launches into the song with all his heart and lungs, following a syncopated rhythm; his vocal delivery is intentionally jagged, full of deliberate pauses and breaks, and in those gaps, a different path is paved: the path of Starsailor, his finest album, a record that could take him all the way up to the clouds, where it never rains.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The phrase "Changing Horses" has always evoked images for me of "turning the page," or a need to slow down and gain perspective, to view things from a different angle and perhaps clarify a change in direction. It feels like a self-imposed exercise in clarity. And I always sensed great wisdom in the music of this sixth album by The Incredible String Band, by then firmly established as a quartet.It begins quietly and without grand ambition with a country-tinged track called "Big Ted," which later shifts into a boogie style. "White Bird" feels almost like a recited poem, even though it is sung by Mike Heron, accompanied by flute, organ, and guitar, and that simplicity lends it a power... one that is further enhanced by the inclusion of the choir. Vocal layering was one of the band's strengths, and it is beautifully realized here. There is a moment where the track pauses, leaving just the guitar improvising notes'almost at random'and therein lies another kind of sonic power: out of nowhere, he finds a very specific, strong melody (which was undoubtedly already in his head) yet makes it seem spontaneous... seamlessly segueing into the next section of "White Bird."In addition to its catchy chorus, "Dust Be Diamonds" makes excellent use of the vibraphone and features instruments that mirror the melody during the chorus. "Sleepers, Awake!" is another example, one of the best, of their vocal harmonies, which conveyed not just musicality, but the harmony that reigned between them at the time. With nothing but their voices, they could reach both luminous and dark corners at will."Mr. and Mrs." is an evocative melody, intriguing and mysterious, featuring a touch of Bossa Nova guitar before shifting into a medieval sound, transporting the listener to the Druid forest that was their natural habitat. Out of nowhere, the tempo could quicken and take on a bluesy feel; that hippie spirit they embodied held layers and nuances, varying heights like the pines in a forest, just as their music could evolve, becoming psychedelic and even slightly funky at times, only to turn overwhelmingly simple and deeply moving."Creation" is the album's centerpiece; here, the band draws upon its most experimental Indian music roots, incorporating choir, percussion, sitar, and tabla, to offer a journey that literally transports the listener. This was another of the quartet's strengths, aided here by Ivan Pawle on organ and piano. It feels like witnessing an occult ritual, something meant for the few, perhaps even incognito, hidden away amidst the forest.When they chose to, they could display virtuosity, with the guitar accelerating to match the rhythm of the tabla, while the spoken-word vocals lend the track a prophetic air.The theme is creation, and every element is present: the chaos, that moment before form takes shape, like an incandescent mass of liquid lava that darkens as it cools and hardens into solid rock, all embodied by that choir and that endless sitar. Next comes a unique piano-driven section that shifts the very ground beneath one's feet (both back then and still today when listening to the record). Finally, the track gives way to a bluesy, tavern-style finish; the journey's circle was both completed and broken, and that was precisely the intention: to break the cycle in order to move forward. The future would bring the musical U and many more adventures.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Aether, created in 2021 by four friends, initially began as a project for bassist Andrea's final thesis, with the aim of moving away from conventional jazzy sounds. Their sound blends post-rock, contemporary classical rock, and multi-layered jazzy prog."Oort Cloud" is a prime example, fusing ambient, jazzy tones, and dino-tinged progressive rock reminiscent of King Crimson, with a flute buzzing here and there. A long, contemplative suite encourages a dreamlike journey, with a primal Fender Rhodes piano accompanying the oppressive psychedelic guitar riff. "Vogon" opens with Collins' electronic drums, then shifts to a jazzier feel with Claudio Milano's frenetic narration. The air soars on Zappa-esque jazz-rock guitar in the purest tradition, flirting with the great Return To Forever on the distinctive piano; a frenetic finale with infectious energy. "Five Shades, Four Frames" opens with a spacey sound, a prominent rhythmic bassline. A drift into hyperspace follows this encroaching Crimson-esque crescendo; improvisation steers clear of interstellar notes. Midway through, the sound takes on an Arabic quality, reminiscent of a Star Wars desert, over a psychedelic Tangerine Dream melody. The obvious jazzy Rhodes turn on a drumbeat with a hint of Steven Wilson is surprising."The Melancholy of the Little Prince" features a melancholic piano drifting over percussion and electronic notes, giving free rein to the fretless bass. Musical scales, a crackling, distorted sound as if from a parallel universe. "Panta Rei" sees the flute searching for its footing, wandering notes for a learned musical digression; jazz, unmistakably King Crimson, Andrea's guitar surfing avant-garde territory for a controlled jumble. Dynamic and apocalyptic with its explosive contemporary finale, "Swerve" opens with a snowy, religious, ethereal feel. The captivating keyboards lead into post-rock territory illuminated by scores reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. The track then veers into jazzy soft rock territory with a distinctive piano demon unleashing a fury, recounting the new Italian sound.Aether brilliantly dares to create a jazzy post-rock fusion, injecting a dose of ambient and modern prog, opening this movement to the contemporary world.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After debuting in 2021 with one of Brazil's strangest contributions to the world of zeuhl metal, theJo�o Pessoa based PAPANGU jettisoned the metallic edge of its debut "Holocene" with its follow up"Lampi�o Rei" which followed in 2024 with more of a classic progressive rock approach mixed with thesounds of Brazil ranging from forro, xaxado and udigrudi. The band returns with its Brazilianbravado cocktail of prog and local flavors with its third installment CELESTIAL which features a 10-track concept that once again steers its sound into a new direction. Trimming down from a sextet toa five-member outfit, CELESTIAL follows suit with the metal aspects deemphasized (although stillpresent) and more retro warmth evoked through the use of analog equipment and a passion for bringingthe likes of jazz fusion, symphonic prog, zeuhl and other classic prog influences to this Brazilianstreet party.Another main feature of this third musical expedition is that on CELESTIAL the vocals are ratherdownplayed with crafty instrumental complexities nurturing warm inviting melodies into displays ofprog majesty evoking the elegance of 70s jazz fusion, the artifice of Gentle Giant complexities andthe sneaky labyrinthine excursionist proclivities that nurtured intuited perspicacity throughmusical obstacle courses that never lose their soul and of course all fortified with the true joiede vie that only Brazilian musical styles can deliver. It's a triumphant return to a new form afterwhat sounded to me like a clunky and disjointed sophomore offering. More focused and refined,CELESTIAL may not deliver the supposed concept of a bandit on a mission to prevent an ecologicaldisaster in some undisclosed form but for what the story narrative lacks in heft, the musicalprowess more than compensates for.CELESTIAL may share an album title with the post-metal band Isis but delivers a truer musical vibeof heavenly bliss with the Rhodes piano and vintage keyboard sounds leading the way. Add someunexpected sound effects from a rubber chicken and Brazilian folk instruments and it's easy to getsucked into the majesty of CELESTIAL's intricate flow of modern modern meets retro with a sensiblerunning time of just over 50 minutes. The album's energy bursts into full gear on the opening "Mau-Olhado" and continues its journey of jubilee throughout the album's ten distinct installments. Awaft of classic Canterbury is present throughout evoking the warmth of that classic Egg / SoftMachine / Hatfield & The North along with occasional bursts of heavier rock that emulates blackmetal (at least in the vocal department) all creatively wrapped in the retro prog padding that keepsthe album amazingly well balanced.Tracks like "Fechamento de Corpo" exhibit the band's menagerie of modernity with staccato basedgrooves fortified with crazy contrapuntal effects and a zeuhl-esque propulsion system that allowsthe cadences and motifs to cozy up together snuggly like a den of hibernating mammals. While theprevious works had me wondering if PAPANGU was primarily a one hit wonder with its out of the gatecrashing the prog party debut, CELESTIAL puts those concerns to rest with a beautifully deliveredprocession of tones and timbres executed in crafty compositions that find the band a form ofmaturation that seemed to be lost on "Lampi�o Rei." Throughout this smorgasbord of retro prog onecan detect moments of classic Yes, Genesis, Gentle Giant, Weather Report, Egg and the list goes onhowever PAPANGU also ekes out modernities with excellent production value and 21st century jazzplaybook tricks. While the metal felt out of balance on the previous album, here the subordinateeffects are instigated perfectly without the bombast ruining the dynamic flow. A brilliant thirdalbum here!
